A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

derivations.claim: The positive-weight support is nonempty by [F1]. List its finitely many distinct score values in decreasing order as $t_1>\cdots>t_m$, let $d_j=\sum_{T(\omega)=t_j}w(\omega)>0$, and put $a_0=0$ and $a_j=\sum_{k=1}^j d_k$. These cumulative masses satisfy $0=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_m=1$.

If $T(Z)=t_j$, then $q(Z)=a_j$. For $u<1$, the indices with $a_j\le u$ form an initial segment; if its last index is $j_0$, then $\Pr(q(Z)\le u)=\sum_{j\le j_0}d_j=a_{j_0}\le u$, while an empty segment has probability zero. At $u=1$ the probability is one. Thus $q(Z)$ is superuniform.

On the score level $t_j$, the strict-tail mass is $a_{j-1}$ and the tied mass is $d_j$, so $q^+(Z,U)=a_{j-1}+Ud_j$. By [A1], conditional on this score level its probability of being at most $u$ is zero for $u\le a_{j-1}$, $(u-a_{j-1})/d_j$ for $a_{j-1}<u<a_j$, and one for $u\ge a_j$.

Multiplying these conditional probabilities by $d_j$ gives the lengths of $[a_{j-1},a_j]\cap[0,u]$. These consecutive intervals partition $[0,1]$, so their lengths sum to $u$. Therefore $\Pr(q^+(Z,U)\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: The finite probability space has nonempty positive-weight support because the weights sum to one; no conclusion is claimed for an empty space.
Step 1.1 orders only positive-mass score levels. Zero-weight assignments contribute nothing to either tail sum and cause no division.
Statement: With a single positive-mass score level, $a_1=d_1=1$, so $q(Z)=1$ and $q^+(Z,U)=U$; the stated bounds hold.
Statement: If all positive-mass outcomes have the same score, there is one score level and the preceding one-level calculation applies.
Statement: step 2.1 treats u=1 explicitly; step 3.1 covers u=0 and u=1 in the partition-of-[0,1] calculation.
Statement: The proof orders finitely many real score values and uses finite sums only; it uses no choice axiom.

citations.quote:
Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent. Their values are
**substantively untestable** from the observed-data law; the
assignment-invariance claim is a hypothesis tested by the theorem, not an
empirical fact supplied by the design. These classifications do not make
the design or scientific model empirically true.

In the finite randomized treatment-assignment model
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]], a schedule satisfies
the **Fisher sharp null** when for each unit $i$ there is a value $y_i$ such that
$Y_i(z)=y_i$ for every allowed assignment $z$. The full vector
$y=(y_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$ is then imputable under every assignment.

A **predeclared ordering score** is a real-valued statistic
$T:\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}\to\mathbb R$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) fixed before the
assignment and outcomes are inspected. Its upper-tail ordering includes ties:
assignment $z'$ is at least as extreme as $z$ when $T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)$.
For a signed score $S$ and fixed null center $s_0$, the corresponding
two-sided ordering is explicitly $T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$; for a no-effect
sharp null the center is $s_0=0$. A lower-tail ordering is represented by
using $-S$ as the score. A statistic in this setting is a measurable map in
the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; the full power-set data
sigma-algebra makes every such real-valued map measurable.

Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space, let $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$,
and let $Z$ have law $w$. Define
$$q(z):=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)1\{T(\omega)\ge T(z)\}.$$
Then $\Pr(q(Z)\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$. If an auxiliary random
variable $U$ is independent of $Z$ and uniform on $[0,1]$, define
$$q^+(Z,U):=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)1\{T(\omega)>T(Z)\}+U\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)1\{T(\omega)=T(Z)\}.$$
Then $\Pr(q^+(Z,U)\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Consider the no-interference binary-treatment submodel of
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]] in which the allowed
assignment set is $\{0,1\}^{\mathcal I}$ and unit $i$'s response under
assignment vector $z$ is $Y_i(z)=Y_i(z_i)$ for fixed real potential responses
$Y_i(0)$ and $Y_i(1)$. For the fixed units, define the
**finite-population average treatment effect** by
$$\tau_F:=\frac1N\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\bigl(Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\bigr).$$
The **weak zero-average-effect null** is the hypothesis $\tau_F=0$; it
constrains the average of the unit-level effects, not each effect separately.
The Fisher sharp null in this submodel, defined in
[[def-fisher-sharp-null-and-predeclared-test-orderings]], requires
$Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)$ for every unit. No probability distribution on the fixed
potential responses is part of either definition.

derivations.claim: The schedule with $Y_i(z)=0$ for every unit and assignment belongs to the Fisher sharp null, so its null class is nonempty as required by [F4]. Fix any sharp-null schedule $\theta$ and choose its common response vector $y$ by [F2]. For every realized assignment $Z$, the observed vector $Y_\theta(Z)$ equals $y$, and every assignment score $T(z,y)$ is therefore imputable.

The formula $p_{\rm rand}(z,y)$ is a finite sum of selected nonnegative assignment weights, so it lies in $[0,1]$. It is a statistic because the data space has its full power-set sigma-algebra, so every preimage is measurable by [F5]. On the product extension with law $\widetilde P_\theta=P_\theta\otimes\lambda$, $p^+$ is a finite combination of score comparisons on the finite assignment space and the measurable coordinate $U$, so it is measurable and its value lies between zero and the total assignment mass one.

On this fixed schedule set $T_y(z)=T(z,y)$. Substituting $Y_\theta(Z)=y$ from step 1.1 into the two displayed formulas identifies $p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ and $p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)$ with the two finite weighted rank transforms of [F3] on $(\mathcal Z,p)$, using [A1] for the tie-randomized transform. Hence $P_\theta(p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))\le u)\le u$ and $\widetilde P_\theta(p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

Since the bound holds for every schedule in the sharp null, [F4] makes $p_{\rm rand}$ a valid p-value for that null. The randomized value is uniform under each extended law $\widetilde P_\theta$, and therefore is also superuniform there; its threshold rule has null rejection probability at most its threshold. No step uses an error distribution. By [F2] and [F6], the argument covers a weak average-effect schedule only when it also satisfies the sharp null.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: The model requires a nonempty assignment space, and the sharp-null parameter class is nonempty because constant outcome schedules exist.
Statement: Zero-weight assignments are permitted by the model, appear with zero contribution in the weighted sums, and require no division.
Statement: A singleton assignment law reduces to the one-score case of [F3], giving $p_{\rm rand}=1$ and $p^+=U$.
Statement: If all positive-probability assignments have the same score, the inclusive p-value is one and randomized ties give the supplied uniform variable.
Statement: The theorem and [F3] include $u=0$ and $u=1$; the inclusive p-value bound holds at both endpoints.
Statement: The reduction uses only the finite assignment space, fixed schedule, and finite weighted-tail lemma. It assumes no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Under the stated no-interference schedule, unit 1's treatment effect is $Y_1(1)-Y_1(0)=1$, while unit 2's is $Y_2(1)-Y_2(0)=-1$. Their finite-population average from [F2] is $(1+(-1))/2=0$. The four assignment weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so they define a valid finite assignment law.

But $Y_1(0,0)=0\ne1=Y_1(1,0)$ and $Y_2(0,0)=0\ne-1=Y_2(0,1)$. Thus both units' responses vary across allowed assignments, contrary to [F3]. The average-effect null [F2] does not imply the Fisher sharp null.

derivations.claim: The assignment weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and each unit's outcome is the same under all three assignments, so this is a finite assignment law satisfying the Fisher sharp null.
If unit 1, 2, or 3 is treated, the signed differences are respectively $0-(1+2)/2=-3/2$, $1-(0+2)/2=0$, and $2-(0+1)/2=3/2$. The two-sided scores are therefore $3/2,0,3/2$.

Each outer assignment has inclusive upper-tail mass $1/2+1/6=2/3$; the middle score is the minimum, so its inclusive upper-tail mass is $1$. The nonrandomized p-value therefore equals $2/3$ with probability $2/3$ and $1$ with probability $1/3$. Its distribution function is $0$ below $2/3$, $2/3$ on $[2/3,1)$, and $1$ at $1$, which is at most its argument throughout $[0,1]$.

At either outer assignment the strict-tail mass is zero and the tied mass is $2/3$, so $p^+=(2/3)U$. At the middle assignment the strict-tail mass is $2/3$ and the tied mass is $1/3$, so $p^+=2/3+U/3$.

For $0\le u\le2/3$, the outer assignments contribute $(2/3)P(U\le 3u/2)=u$. For $2/3\le u\le1$, they contribute $2/3$ and the middle assignment contributes $(1/3)P(U\le3u-2)=u-2/3$; hence $P(p^+\le u)=u$ on the entire unit interval. Together with step 3.1, this verifies the theorem's superuniform and uniform conclusions for this assignment law.
